entries.title: Laibach and NSK, over-identification
text: The Slovene band Laibach and the collective around it took the opposite road to irony. Their statement of 1982: “All art is subject to political manipulation, except for that which speaks the language of this same manipulation.” Slavoj Žižek called the strategy over-identification: Laibach “‘frustrates’ the system (the ruling ideology) precisely insofar as it is not its ironic imitation, but over-identification with it”.

In 1987 their designers won Yugoslavia's Day of Youth poster competition with an entry based on a Nazi painting of 1936, its symbols replaced with Yugoslav ones. The objection to this project: ironic distance may be exactly what such systems can live with. A lead on two details of the Žižek reference.
facts: What it is: the strategy of the Slovene band Laibach and of Neue Slowenische Kunst, founded in 1984 by Laibach, Irwin and the Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre, which Slavoj Žižek called over-identification (Zdenka Badovinac, 'over-identification', glossary of common knowledge, May 2015, MG+MSUM, https://glossary.internationaleonline.org/referential-fields/subjectivisation/over-identification, read in the Wayback copy of 21 April 2025; the live page refused access).

Chat: 'Žižek argued in 1993 ...' Not found on https://glossary.internationaleonline.org/referential-fields/subjectivisation/over-identification: it places Žižek's characterisation 'About a decade later' than Laibach's 1982 statement and refers to 'his writings from the late 1980s and early 1990s'; no year 1993, no essay title.

Chat: '... that ironic distance had become the condition for the system to function.' Not found in those words on the glossary page. Closest: 'There is no need to underline how irony and criticism best serve the system itself', and Žižek's point that critics assumed 'that ironic distance is automatically subversive'.

Chat: 'Laibach frustrates the system by refusing that distance.' Confirmed by the glossary, quoting Žižek: Laibach '’frustrates’ the system (the ruling ideology) precisely insofar as it is not its ironic imitation, but over-identification with it'.
Chat's own reading, not a statement of fact: 'It’s the opposite strategy to yours.'

Symbols, per the glossary: Laibach's 1982 statement, 'All art is subject to political manipulation, except for that which speaks the language of this same manipulation'; in 1987 NSK's design group New Collectivism won the Yugoslav Day of Youth poster competition with an entry based on a 1936 Nazi painting, its Nazi symbols replaced with Yugoslav ones.
Picture: Wikimedia Commons, 'Die Volksbühne Berlin als NSK-Staat Berlin', 1993, Gruppe LAIBACH, CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NSK_STAAT_Berlin_1993.jpg).

Seen in the image: a black-and-white photograph of the Volksbühne, its curved façade lettered 'VOLKSBÜHNE' above tall columns; two long dark banners hang at either side, each with a round emblem and the letters 'NSK'.

images.caption: Gruppe LAIBACH, the Volksbühne Berlin as 'NSK-Staat Berlin', 1993. CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

source.label: Zdenka Badovinac, 'over-identification', glossary of common knowledge (Internationale Online), May 2015

entries.creator: Laibach / Neue Slowenische Kunst; the concept named by Slavoj Žižek

confidence.note: The year 1993 and 'condition for the system to function' were not found on the glossary page (read in its Wayback copy of 21 April 2025); 'frustrates the system' is confirmed.

entries.title: Wang Guangyi, Great Criticism
text: A series of paintings, 1990 to 2007, in which the figures of Cultural Revolution posters, Red Guards, workers and peasants in black outline on red and yellow, are set against the logos of Coca-Cola, Dior and Chanel, each “in its trademark typeface”. Two visual languages of persuasion are laid over each other, and neither is altered.
The critic Li Xianting saw “a humorous and absurd effect”. The painter disagreed: the conflict “cannot be dissolved through irony or sarcasm”.
facts: What it is: Wang Guangyi's painting series Great Criticism, his best-known cycle, which combines Cultural Revolution imagery with Western consumer brands (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Guangyi).

Chat: 'Wang Guangyi, Great Criticism (1990–2007).' Confirmed by https://roguearthistorian.substack.com/p/from-red-guards-to-red-labels-ideology: 'His Great Criticism series (1990–2007)'; Wikipedia's section heading also reads 'Great Criticism, 1990-2007' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Guangyi).

Chat: 'Cultural Revolution Red Guards, workers and peasants are laid over Coca-Cola, Dior and Chanel logos.' Confirmed by https://roguearthistorian.substack.com/p/from-red-guards-to-red-labels-ideology: the series 'superimposes Cultural Revolution propaganda figures, Red Guards, workers, peasants, onto global brand logos such as Coca-Cola, Dior, and Chanel'.

Form, per the same post: each work has 'monochrome propaganda figures ... rendered against a flat field of red' and 'a Western logo in its trademark typeface, typically white on red'; first shown internationally at the 45th Venice Biennale in 1993 (Rogue Art Historian, 27 May 2025).

Origin, per Wikipedia: Wang 'caught sight of a cigarettes pack lying on an old political poster'; Great Criticism: Coca-Cola was on the cover of Flash Art in 1992 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Guangyi).

Two readings, both on Wikipedia: Li Xianting sees 'a humorous and absurd effect that yet carries with it an implied cultural criticism'; Wang says the conflict 'cannot be dissolved through irony or sarcasm' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Guangyi).
Picture: captioned 'Guangyi, Great Criticism: Coca-Cola' on the Rogue Art Historian post, with no year, medium or credit (manifest).

Seen in the image: three stern figures drawn in black outline on yellow, one in a cap with a red star, grip a giant fountain pen against red and yellow fields; white 'Coca-Cola' script on a red band at bottom right; stencilled rows of '1234567890' scattered over the whole canvas.

images.caption: Wang Guangyi, Great Criticism: Coca-Cola (year not given). No image credit on the page; as shown on Rogue Art Historian (Substack), 2025.

source.label: Rogue Art Historian, 'From Red Guards to Red Labels: Ideology, Iconography, and Consumerism in Great Criticism', 27 May 2025

entries.creator: Wang Guangyi
entries.rights: No image credit on the page; site footer '© 2026 Rogue Art Historian'

entries.title: Serdar Somuncu reads Mein Kampf
text: From 1996 Serdar Somuncu toured Germany reading from Mein Kampf on stage, to show, in one description, “the absurdity of Hitler's propaganda”: “education by satire”. Officials in Schwerin and Ingolstadt tried to stop the shows, and threats from neo-Nazis made him wear a bullet-proof vest. The text is unchanged. What changes is the voice that reads it.
The numbers differ by source. His publisher counts six years, more than 1,500 performances and half a million spectators; another account gives 1,428 readings and 250,000.
facts: What it is: Serdar Somuncu's scenic readings from Hitler's Mein Kampf, begun in 1996; the picture is the cover of his 2015 book about them, Der Adolf in mir. Die Karriere einer verbotenen Idee (WortArt, ISBN 978-3-942454-17-9) (https://www.wortart-shop.de/kuenstler/serdar-somuncu/serdar-somuncu-der-adolf-in-mir-die-karriere-einer-verbotenen-idee-buch).

Chat: 'Starting in 1996, he spent six years on stage, with over 1,500 performances for more than half a million people.' Confirmed by the publisher's text on https://www.wortart-shop.de/kuenstler/serdar-somuncu/serdar-somuncu-der-adolf-in-mir-die-karriere-einer-verbotenen-idee-buch: '1996 begann Serdar Somuncu seine spektakuläre und ganze sechs Jahre andauernde szenische Lesereise mit Adolf Hitlers Mein Kampf. Mit mehr als 1.500 Auftritten vor über einer halben Million Zuschauern'.

Chat: 'Local officials in some cities tried to stop the shows.' Confirmed by https://freespeechdebate.com/case/hitlers-mein-kampf-as-satire/ (read in the Wayback copy of 2 August 2024; the live site refused connection): 'In German cities such as Schwerin and Ingolstadt, local government officials from various political parties tried to prevent Somuncu from performing'.

Conflict: the same Free Speech Debate case (Sebastian Huempfer, 13 July 2012) gives other figures: the show toured 'From 1991 until 2001', 'more than 1,428 readings', 'a total audience of 250,000'. Qantara gives 1996 for the first reading and 'over 1,500 performances' (https://qantara.de/en/article/serdar-somuncu-hitler-kebab-eye-opener-without-taboos).

Free Speech Debate on the form: Somuncu 'recites excerpts from Adolf Hitler’s book Mein Kampf to highlight the absurdity of Hitler’s propaganda'; 'Somuncu’s show is education by satire'; he was 'repeatedly forced to wear a bullet-proof vest' because of neo-Nazi threats.

The page the chat named (Lesejury, 'Der Adolf in mir') was down for maintenance on 10 November 2026 (HTTP 503); Goodreads carries the same publisher text as WortArt (https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/27232408).

Seen in the image: book cover; a close-up of a bearded man's face lit red, a toothbrush held under his nose like a small moustache; 'DER ADOLF IN MIR' in large white capitals, subtitle 'Die Karriere einer verbotenen Idee', 'SERDAR SOMUNCU' at top, the WortArt logo at bottom.

images.caption: Cover of Serdar Somuncu, Der Adolf in mir (WortArt, 2015). No image credit; shop footer 'Copyright © wortart-shop.de - Alle Rechte vorbehalten'.

source.label: WortArt shop, 'Serdar Somuncu - Der Adolf in mir - Die Karriere einer verbotenen Idee - Buch'

entries.creator: Serdar Somuncu
entries.rights: No image credit; shop footer 'Copyright © wortart-shop.de - Alle Rechte vorbehalten'

confidence.note: Every statement confirmed: the figures on the publisher's (WortArt) page, the officials on Free Speech Debate (Wayback copy). The two disagree: 1996, six years, 1,500+ shows, 500,000+ spectators against 1991–2001, 1,428 readings, 250,000.

entries.title: Manga de Dokuha: Mein Kampf and Das Kapital as manga
text: A Japanese series that retells classic books as manga. Its Mein Kampf of 2008 sold 45,000 copies, above the series' average, and Das Kapital followed, told through the owner of a cheese factory. The Bavarian finance ministry said: “We have trouble considering manga as an appropriate medium for critically presenting this problematic material.” The editor's argument was that the book is well known and little read.
The reference chat's verdict: a change of format that arguably popularizes instead of defusing.
facts: What it is: Manga de Dokuha ('Reading Through with Manga'), a series of manga adaptations of classic works, East Press 2007–17 and later Gakken; Kosuke Maruo produces each book, artwork by Variety Art Works (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga_de_Dokuha).

Chat: 'The series published Das Kapital and Mein Kampf as manga.' Confirmed by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga_de_Dokuha: 'East Press published best-selling versions of the communist novel Kanikōsen, Karl Marx's Das Kapital and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf.'

Chat: 'The Mein Kampf volume sold 45,000 copies.' Confirmed by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga_de_Dokuha ('selling 45,000 copies') and https://www.animenewsnetwork.com/news/2009-09-06/manga-version-of-hitler-mein-kampf-sells-45000 ('sold 45,000 copies since last November', above the series average of 35,000).

Chat: '... and drew criticism from Bavaria.' Confirmed by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga_de_Dokuha: the Bavarian Finance Ministry 'issued a statement saying that manga was an inappropriate medium for Hitler's writing'; ANN quotes it: 'We have trouble considering manga as an appropriate medium for critically presenting this problematic material.'

Chat's own reading, not a statement of fact: 'It's a format change that arguably popularizes rather than defuses.' The editor Maruo, per Wikipedia: 'Mein Kampf is a well-known book, but relatively few people have read it.'
Voice: Das Kapital is retold 'via the fictionalized tale of Robin, the owner of a cheese factory' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga_de_Dokuha).
Dates differ: Wikipedia's text gives October 2008 for Mein Kampf, its own list November 2008 (MD024), ANN 'since last November'; Das Kapital is MD027, December 2008 (Wikipedia).

Seen in the image: a black-and-white manga double page in panels with Japanese speech balloons; close-ups of a dark-haired young man, a woman holding a small child at top left, a man reading on a park bench at bottom right.

images.caption: Manga de Dokuha, Mein Kampf (East Press, 2008), a double page. No caption or credit; as shown by Anime News Network, 6 September 2009.

entries.creator: East Press (producer Kosuke Maruo; artwork Variety Art Works)
entries.rights: No caption or credit on the page (Anime News Network)

confidence.note: Every factual statement confirmed on Wikipedia, 'Manga de Dokuha', and Anime News Network (6 September 2009); 'popularizes rather than defuses' is the chat's opinion; the month of the Mein Kampf volume differs (October or November 2008).

entries.title: Hate Poetry
text: An “antirassistische Leseshow” that ran from 2012 to 2015. German journalists of non-German background read aloud the racist letters their readers send them, as a contest for the worst, with music and confetti. Die Welt: “Selten war Rassismus so unterhaltsam.”

Martin Seel explained in the Süddeutsche Zeitung why it works: “Die Journalisten nehmen ja die rassistischen Kommentare genau dadurch ernst, dass sie sie nicht zu ernst nehmen.” The letters are read by the people they were meant to wound, in front of an audience that laughs.
facts: What it is: Hate Poetry, an 'antirassistische Leseshow' in which German journalists of non-German background read racist letters to the editor aloud in the style of a poetry slam; idea Ebru Taşdemir; first held in January 2012 at the taz-Café, Berlin; the series ended in 2015 (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_Poetry).

Chat: 'Journalists including Amjahid, Gezer, Kazim, Kiyak, Musharbash, Topçu and Yücel read out their most memorable hate mail.' Confirmed by https://www.hebbel-am-ufer.de/en/programme/pdetail/hate-poetry: 'Mohamed Amjahid (Tagesspiegel), Özlem Gezer (Spiegel), Hasnain Kazim (Spiegel), Mely Kiyak (Gorki Theatre, freelance writer), Yassin Musharbash (Zeit), Özlem Topçu (Zeit) and Deniz Yücel (taz) read from their most memorable letters.'

Format, per HAU: 'A contest for the most racist letters to the editor', moderated by Doris Akrap (taz), music by Malek Samo (live); HAU1, Sunday 15 February 2015, 180–240 minutes (https://www.hebbel-am-ufer.de/en/programme/pdetail/hate-poetry).

Reception, as quoted on German Wikipedia: Die Welt, 'Selten war Rassismus so unterhaltsam'; the taz, a 'kathartische Lesung'; Martin Seel in the Süddeutsche Zeitung: 'Die Journalisten nehmen ja die rassistischen Kommentare genau dadurch ernst, dass sie sie nicht zu ernst nehmen.' (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_Poetry).

Seen in the image: a dark stage with a long table of readers behind microphones, its front hung with flags and pinned with portrait photographs; white balloons, confetti and a small fringed rug on the floor in front; flags on the back wall.

images.caption: Hate Poetry on stage, photograph by Dorothea Tuch (date not stated). © Photographer Dorothea Tuch; HAU Hebbel am Ufer programme page.

source.label: HAU Hebbel am Ufer, programme page 'Hate Poetry'

entries.creator: Ebru Taşdemir (idea), with Mohamed Amjahid, Özlem Gezer, Hasnain Kazim, Mely Kiyak, Yassin Musharbash, Özlem Topçu, Deniz Yücel; moderation Doris Akrap

entries.title: Rechts gegen Rechts, the involuntary walkathon, Wunsiedel
text: In November 2014 the annual neo-Nazi march in Wunsiedel was turned, by a group calling itself Rechts gegen Rechts, into “Germany's most involuntary walkathon”. For every metre the marchers walked, sponsors gave ten euros to EXIT-Deutschland, which helps people leave the far right. Signs along the route cheered them on, and a table of bananas stood under the sign “Mein Mampf”. The march raised 10,000 euros against itself.
Nothing about the march was changed except what it was called. EXIT's own journal says the rate was per kilometre; the banner in the picture says per metre.
facts: What it is: the neo-Nazi march in Wunsiedel of 15 November 2014, turned by the group Rechts gegen Rechts into a sponsored walk for EXIT-Deutschland, a group that helps people leave the far right (https://www.thelocal.de/20141117/charity-turns-neo-nazi-march-into-fundraiser-wunseidel).

Chat: 'The annual neo-Nazi march became an “involuntary walkathon”.' Confirmed by https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-news/neo-nazis-tricked-into-raising-thousands-for-anti-extremism-charity-168193/: Rechts gegen Rechts tried a new tactic, 'hosting what they called Germany’s “most involuntary walkathon.”'

Chat: '... sponsored at €10 per metre.' Confirmed by Rolling Stone ('pledge €10 for every meter they walked') and The Local ('Every metre they walked, an additional €10'). Conflict: EXIT-Deutschland's own journal says 'ten euros would be donated ... for every kilometer' (https://journal-exit.de/nazis-against-nazis/); the start banner in the picture says per metre.

Chat: 'There were motivational signs and a “Mein Mampf” banana stand.' Confirmed by Rolling Stone: 'hanging “motivational” signs throughout the route (“If only the Führer knew!,” ...)' and 'A table of bananas was left out with the pun-tastic sign, “Mein Mampf”'.

Chat: '... it raised €10,000 for Exit.' Confirmed by Rolling Stone: 'a walkathon that raised 10,000 euros for an anti-extremist organization'; The Local: '€10,000 raised by the marchers completing their walk'.

Wording on the route, per EXIT: posters with 'right against the right', 'Germany’s most involuntary walkathon', 'goosestepping for donations' and 'the ultimate sprint instead of the ultimate victory'; at the finish 'Thank you sports fans! 10,000 euros will now go to EXIT Germany' (https://journal-exit.de/nazis-against-nazis/).

Seen in the image: police in green uniforms and a crowd behind a fence at left; at right a large white banner with coloured confetti dots, a pink disc reading 'RECHTS gegen RECHTS', a blue disc reading 'Der unfreiwilligste Spendenlauf Deutschlands', and the line 'Für jeden Meter gehen 10 € an EXIT-Deutschland.'; The Local's caption: 'The starting line.'

images.caption: Rechts gegen Rechts, start banner, Wunsiedel, November 2014. 'Photo courtesy Rechts-gegen-rechts', The Local.

entries.title: #ISISクソコラグランプリ (ISIS crappy collage grand prix)
text: In January 2015, after a hostage video threatening two Japanese men, Japanese Twitter users answered under a hashtag meaning “ISIS crappy collage grand prix”: tens of thousands of absurd edits of the video's stills. They seized on the look of the footage, whose desert background appeared to be pasted in. It was criticised at the time as insensitive while two lives were at stake.
The picture is one of the edits, the masked figure cut out and set on a video-game title card. The video itself was not saved.
facts: What it is: a Japanese Twitter hashtag of January 2015 under which users posted mocking photoshopped versions of an IS hostage video released on 20 January 2015 that threatened Kenji Goto and Haruna Yukawa (https://meme.com/memes/isis-crappy-collage-grand-prix; Kotaku, 21 January 2015, https://kotaku.com/japanese-twitter-users-stand-up-to-isis-with-a-photos-1680848705).

Chat: 'Japanese Twitter users flooded the ISIS hostage-video stills with absurd photoshops.' Confirmed by https://meme.com/memes/isis-crappy-collage-grand-prix: users 'responded to an ISIS hostage video by flooding the hashtag with absurd, mocking Photoshop edits of the footage'; Al Jazeera: 'Japanese netizens mocked the hostage video using photoshopped memes' (https://www.aljazeera.com/video/the-stream/2015/1/21/japanese-tweeters-mock-isil-hostage-video).

Chat: '... exploiting the obviously composited desert background.' Confirmed by https://meme.com/memes/isis-crappy-collage-grand-prix: 'The meme exploited the fact that the original video's desert background looked obviously composited.' Al Jazeera gives it only as a suspicion: 'visual inconsistencies suggested it may have been filmed using a green screen to place a fake background'.

Counts differ by source and day: Al Jazeera 'more than 50,000 uses', Dazed '75,000 times', NBC News 'more than 60,000 times', meme.com '220,000+' (https://www.dazeddigital.com/artsandculture/article/23349/1/why-japan-is-mocking-isis-with-photoshopped-twitter-memes; https://www.nbcnews.com/storyline/isis-terror/japanese-twitter-users-mock-isis-internet-meme-n291591).

Criticised at the time as insensitive while two lives were at stake: 'there are certainly Japanese Twitter users who find the Photoshop meme “imprudent.”' (Kotaku); Dazed: 'criticised as insensitive by some'.

Picture: one of the edits, credited by Know Your Meme to '@KagamineMeltAS7' via Twitter and uploaded there on 22 January 2015, titled 'スマブラに出るってこれマジ？'; Kotaku credits a picture to the same post. No hostages and no IS flag in it; the IS video still itself was not saved (https://knowyourmeme.com/photos/901408-isis-crappy-collage-grand-prix; manifest).
Seen in the image: the black-clad masked figure cut out and set against a blue, starry title card with a black brush stroke and the words 'ISIS 参戦!!' in white and blue lettering.

images.caption: Edit posted under #ISISクソコラグランプリ, January 2015, created by @KagamineMeltAS7 (per Know Your Meme). No licence stated; Know Your Meme.

entries.creator: Japanese Twitter users (pictured edit: @KagamineMeltAS7, per Know Your Meme)
entries.rights: No licence stated; Know Your Meme credits 'Created by @KagamineMeltAS7 via Twitter'

entries.title: Institut für Zeitgeschichte, Hitler, Mein Kampf. Eine kritische Edition
text: The annotated edition of Mein Kampf published by the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in January 2016, as soon as the copyright expired. Hitler's text sits in a block on the right-hand page. More than 3,500 annotations fill the left page and run on beneath it. The institute calls this “a kind of ‘framing’” by which “a subtext to Mein Kampf is constructed”.

The designer, Rudolf Paulus Gorbach, set it in the typeface Scala and took his page grid from a Jewish Bible printed in Venice in 1546 and a Basel edition of Erasmus. A critic wrote that “Hitler's propaganda had to be slowed down”. Here the layout of the page does the work.
facts: What it is: the two-volume critical edition of Mein Kampf by the Institut für Zeitgeschichte München–Berlin, edited by Christian Hartmann, Thomas Vordermayer, Othmar Plöckinger and Roman Töppel, presented in January 2016 right after the copyright expired (https://www.ifz-muenchen.de/en/news/topics/hitler-mein-kampf-a-critical-edition; editors as named on the IfZ press-photo page).

Chat: 'The original text sits on the right-hand page, surrounded by more than 3,500 annotations on the left.' Confirmed by https://languagecollections-blog.lib.cam.ac.uk/2016/05/20/do-you-have-a-copy-of-the-bible-critical-editions-in-the-ul/: 'text on the right-hand page with dated revisions and annotations on the left-hand page', 'more than 3500 annotations'; and by https://www.printmag.com/daily-heller/hitlers-annotated-struggle/: 'The editors concept was to surround Hitler’s text by more than 3,500 comments.'

Chat: 'The institute explicitly calls this framing a way of building a subtext and counter-text.' Confirmed by https://www.ifz-muenchen.de/en/news/topics/hitler-mein-kampf-a-critical-edition: 'By means of a kind of ‘framing’ of the original text in the form of an introduction and detailed commentary, a subtext to Mein Kampf is constructed', and the edition is to offer 'a counter-text to the uncritical and unfiltered dissemination of Hitler’s propaganda'.

Chat: 'The layout was designed by Gorbach Büro für Gestaltung.' Confirmed by https://www.ifz-muenchen.de/en/the-institute/presse/pressematerial-mein-kampf/photos (layout sample credited 'Institut für Zeitgeschichte/Gorbach Büro für Gestaltung') and by https://www.printmag.com/daily-heller/hitlers-annotated-struggle/, which names the designer Rudolf Paulus Gorbach.

Chat's own reading, not a statement of fact: 'This is defusing by page design.' Print (René Spitz, introduced by Steven Heller, 22 February 2016) argues along the same line: 'Hitler’s propaganda had to be slowed down'; the reader 'is not overwhelmed, but stays in a distance' (https://www.printmag.com/daily-heller/hitlers-annotated-struggle/).

Type and grid, per Print: Gorbach 'opted for the type “Scala” of Dutchman Martin Majoor (1993)'; the page grid refers to a Jewish Bible of Venice, 1546, and the Basel edition of Erasmus's Praise of Folly, 1515 (https://www.printmag.com/daily-heller/hitlers-annotated-struggle/).

Seen in the image: the IfZ layout sample, a double page under the heading 'Seitenaufteilung in der Edition Hitler, Mein Kampf' with labelled call-outs; the original text sits in a bold block at the top of the right page with variant notes in its margin; numbered annotations in narrow columns fill the left page and run beneath the original on the right; page numbers 458 and 459.

source.label: Institut für Zeitgeschichte, 'Hitler, Mein Kampf. A Critical Edition'

entries.creator: Institut für Zeitgeschichte (eds. Christian Hartmann, Thomas Vordermayer, Othmar Plöckinger, Roman Töppel); design Rudolf Paulus Gorbach
entries.rights: Picture credits: Institut für Zeitgeschichte/Gorbach Büro für Gestaltung

entries.title: Charlotte Knobloch's objection to the annotated Mein Kampf
text: The objection to the annotated Mein Kampf (the edition is row 12.23). Charlotte Knobloch, a former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, said she worried the new edition would simply awaken interest in the original. The Council itself had no objection, and its president hoped the edition would help in “debunking Hitler's inhuman ideology”. The edition runs to 1,948 pages, roughly twice the original.
This research keeps it because the same doubt applies to every row in this section: a new form also brings the old content back into view.
facts: What it is: the objection of Charlotte Knobloch, a former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, to the critical edition of Mein Kampf, as reported by AP (Michael Faulhaber, Munich, 8 January 2016, https://www.10news.com/news/u-s-world/germany-publishes-annotated-mein-kampf-manifesto-for-1st-time-since-wwii).

Chat: 'Charlotte Knobloch worried the edition would simply awaken interest in the original rather than the commentary.' Confirmed by https://www.10news.com/news/u-s-world/germany-publishes-annotated-mein-kampf-manifesto-for-1st-time-since-wwii: 'One of Schuster's predecessors, Charlotte Knobloch, has said she worries the new edition will simply awaken interest in the original, not the commentary.'

The rest of the debate in the same report: the Central Council 'said it has no objections to the critical edition', and its president Josef Schuster hopes it will 'contribute to debunking Hitler's inhuman ideology and counteracting anti-Semitism'; Ronald Lauder (World Jewish Congress): 'I don't see the need for a critical edition.'

Layout, per the same report: the edition 'sets Hitler's text amid extensive comments by historians that are meant to contradict and deflate his writing' and runs to '1,948 pages, roughly double the original'.
The edition itself is row 12.23; the reference chat types this debate as a counter-reference (chat).
Picture: the edition itself, IfZ press photo 'Edition volumes, upright', a different picture from the layout sample of row 12.23 (manifest).

entries.title: “Gay clown Putin”
text: In spring 2017 Russia's justice ministry put an image of Vladimir Putin in clownish make-up on its list of extremist materials, as number 4,071. The image had circulated at protests against the country's anti-gay laws since 2013.
The ban made it famous. It spread “following reports that the images had been banned”, a Streisand effect. The reference chat's conclusion: regimes take ridicule seriously.
facts: What it is: an image of Vladimir Putin in clownish make-up that Russia's Ministry of Justice put on its list of extremist materials in spring 2017 (The Art Newspaper, 6 April 2017, https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2017/04/06/image-of-putin-made-up-like-a-gay-clown-banned-in-russia).

Chat: 'Russia’s Justice Ministry listed the made-up Putin image as extremist material.' Confirmed by https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2017/04/06/image-of-putin-made-up-like-a-gay-clown-banned-in-russia: 'Russia’s ministry justice has banned an image of Vladimir Putin in clownish make-up ... as “extremist” material'; 'The gay clown poster is now number 4,071 on a list of 4,074 entries.'

Chat: 'The ban spread it further, a Streisand effect.' Confirmed by https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/gay-clown-putin: the images 'were widely circulated online following reports that the images had been banned in Russia in early April 2017, leading many to cite the spread of the images as an example of the Streisand Effect.'

Chat's own reading, not a statement of fact: 'Regimes clearly take ridicule seriously.' The Kremlin's answer, per The Art Newspaper: 'As a person, he might be stung, but as president he is quite resilient to these vulgarities'.

Before the ban: the image 'was one of many that became popular at protests against the country’s anti-gay laws in 2013' (The Art Newspaper); Know Your Meme traces a 'Drag Putin a la Warhol' picture to the Tumblr blog Putin A Rainbow, 9 April 2013, and dates the listing to 30 March 2017.

Picture: The Art Newspaper's header photograph, uncredited on the page; Know Your Meme describes a matching photograph by Denis Doyle (Getty Images) of a demonstrator outside the Russian embassy in Madrid on 23 August 2013; that identification was not checked (manifest).

Seen in the image: two hands hold a printed sheet: Putin's face in pale make-up with heavy black lashes, blue eye shadow and red lips, set before a rainbow, 'STOP HOMOFOBIA' in red capitals across the forehead.

entries.title: The Daily Stormer style guide
text: A counter-example. The leaked style guide of a neo-Nazi website, as excerpted by Harper's Magazine: “Most people are not comfortable with material that comes across as vitriolic, raging, nonironic hatred.” So: “The unindoctrinated should not be able to tell whether we are joking or not.”

Lightness and irony are also how the far right gets its material past people. Whatever this project does with ridicule, the other side has been doing on purpose. Marked as a lead on one phrase the sources do not contain. Read only through reporting.
facts: What it is: the internal style guide of the Daily Stormer, a white-supremacist website, 'reportedly written by Andrew Anglin', obtained by HuffPost as a 17-page document and reported on 13 December 2017 (https://www.huffpost.com/entry/daily-stormer-nazi-style-guide_n_5a2ece19e4b0ce3b344492f2); excerpted in Harper's Magazine, April 2018, Readings (https://harpers.org/archive/2018/04/bearer-of-bad-news/).

Chat: 'It tells writers to keep the tone light ...' Not found on https://harpers.org/archive/2018/04/bearer-of-bad-news/, nor in the text of the HuffPost article, which speaks of 'a veil of irony'; the guide pages HuffPost reproduces as images were not read.

Chat: '... because most people recoil from non-ironic hatred.' Confirmed by https://harpers.org/archive/2018/04/bearer-of-bad-news/: 'Most people are not comfortable with material that comes across as vitriolic, raging, nonironic hatred.'

Chat: '... and to leave readers unsure whether it's a joke.' Confirmed by https://harpers.org/archive/2018/04/bearer-of-bad-news/: 'The unindoctrinated should not be able to tell whether we are joking or not.'

Chat: 'leaked 2017.' Confirmed by https://www.huffpost.com/entry/daily-stormer-nazi-style-guide_n_5a2ece19e4b0ce3b344492f2 (13 December 2017): 'A leaked style guide'; Harper's: 'acquired in December by HuffPost'.

Chat's own reading, not a statement of fact: 'Irony is also a far-right tool, which fits with the Tommy Robinson Comic Sans cover.' HuffPost: 'The Daily Stormer and other groups like it want you to be unsure if you should take them seriously.'
Picture: a screenshot of the Harper's web page, the reporting and not the guide; no image from the guide or from the site was saved (manifest).

Seen in the image: the Harper's Magazine web page: '[Readings]', headline 'Bearer of Bad News', an italic introduction naming the Daily Stormer, Andrew Anglin and HuffPost, the first paragraphs of the excerpt, and the April 2018 cover at right.
